purpose: Species-level admission to the existing scored grass ID key; this is not a voucher, exact-photo identity determination, or county native-range approval. Original source and photo files are immutable.

head.reference: Diggs et al. 1999, printed pp. 1318–1320, Setaria genus and S. viridis account
head.note: A dense Setaria head is subtended by persistent, separate bristles.

habit.reference: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015, printed p. 62, S. viridis account
habit.note: Annual, caespitose/tufted culms; this is a species-level growth-form description.

ligule.reference: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015, printed p. 62, S. viridis account
ligule.note: True ligule a fringe of hairs 1–2 mm, not a ciliate membrane.

awns.reference: Diggs et al. 1999, printed pp. 1318–1320, Setaria genus/species account
awns.note: Sterile bristles subtend the spikelet; the fertile lemma itself is awnless.

remaining_cautions: Foxtail architecture alone cannot distinguish S. viridis from S. pumila or S. parviflora; check mature lemma rugosity and bristle arrangement.
Source-scored species concept; photographs and observations do not certify a Hays County specimen or county nativity.

head.reference: Diggs et al. 1999, printed pp. 1318–1319, S. leucopila account
head.note: Bristled foxtail head; separate bristles below the spikelet.

habit.reference: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015, printed p. 61, S. leucopila account
habit.note: Caespitose perennial, no reported spreading-stolon pathway in the selected basic category.

ligule.reference: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015, printed p. 61, S. leucopila account
ligule.note: Short truncate membranous ligule (~0.5 mm) with cilia 1–2 mm; both first-look membrane and hairs are allowed, NOT a pure hair-fringe diagnosis.

awns.reference: Diggs et al. 1999, printed pp. 1318–1319, Setaria genus and S. leucopila account
awns.note: 1–2 persistent sterile bristles below awnless spikelets; not lemma awns.

remaining_cautions: A ciliate membrane may resemble a hair fringe in the field; inspect beneath the cilia.
Mature fertile lemma details and bristle count help distinguish nearby Setaria; local specimen/nativity not certified.

head.reference: Diggs et al. 1999, printed p. 1290, Oplismenus hirtellus account
head.note: Short flowering branches carry spikelets ranked along one side; rank and side are separate aspects.

habit.reference: Diggs et al. 1999, printed p. 1290, Oplismenus hirtellus account
habit.note: Creeping, decumbent culms root at lower nodes; the field mat category expressly allows rooted decumbent culms, not only stolons.

ligule.reference: Diggs et al. 1999, printed p. 1290, Oplismenus hirtellus account
ligule.note: A ciliate membrane, not an absent ligule; close hairlike rim can justify a first-look hair-fringe impression.

awns.reference: Diggs et al. 1999, printed p. 1290, Oplismenus hirtellus account
awns.note: Long glume awns, notably on the first glume. The main question allows awns of lemma OR glume.

remaining_cautions: Awn attachment on the first glume and the paired spikelet arrangement should be inspected before deciding among Oplismenus relatives.
Source-labeled photographs are teaching references, not a locally verified voucher.

head.reference: Barkworth, Flora of North America, Nassella tenuissima account (online, unpaginated)
head.note: Narrow, loose panicle, with length and enclosure changing with maturity.

habit.reference: Barkworth, Flora of North America, Nassella tenuissima account (online, unpaginated)
habit.note: Densely caespitose perennial, without an inferred rhizome state.

ligule.reference: Barkworth, Flora of North America, Nassella tenuissima account (online, unpaginated)
ligule.note: Membranous ligule approximately 1–5 mm; exact tip shape varies across sources and is not scored.

awns.reference: Barkworth, Flora of North America, Nassella tenuissima account (online, unpaginated)
awns.note: Conspicuous true lemma awns approximately 45–100 mm; twisting/bending varies.

remaining_cautions: Often grown as ornamental Mexican feathergrass; the Lab does NOT classify a Hays County photo as a wild established plant or a verified native occurrence.
Separate from N. leucotricha and other fine-leaved grasses using mature spikelets and awn insertion, not color alone.
